vignette:
Luca Rossi was twenty-eight when the warehouse fire trapped him on the second floor of Brennan Logistics on a Tuesday afternoon in March. He had worked there for eight years, moving steadily from dock associate to supervisor-reliable, punctual, the kind of man his wife Maria called steady. A faulty electrical panel ignited in the storage section where Luca was conducting inventory. The alarm system failed. What he remembers now, with a clarity that exhausts him at thirty-six, is not the full sequence of events but a series of vivid, isolated moments: the smell of accelerant and burning plastic suddenly overwhelming; the sight of a coworker, Derek, deliberately kicking over a stack of pallets to clear an escape route, leaving two junior employees scrambling behind him; the texture of the rough concrete wall he pressed his palms against, searching for a door in the black smoke, feeling that grit embed itself into his skin. Luca made it out through a side window. Derek did not wait for anyone. Two people died in the stairwell.

In the months that followed, Luca told himself the story differently. He had been lucky. The fire was not as bad as the news made it sound. Derek had panicked like anyone would. But these retellings never quite stuck. The moments remained-snapshots, each one sharper than any ordinary memory. When he tried to think of his daughter's sixth birthday party from before the fire, the details were soft, almost watercolor. But the texture of that concrete, Derek's face as he kicked the pallets aside, the sound of the alarm that didn't work-these arrived in his mind with the force of something still happening. The intrusions came without warning: a smell of burnt plastic at a restaurant, the sight of a coworker in a red shirt like Derek had worn, the sound of a fire truck passing on the street. Each time, Luca's body seized as if he were back in the smoke, his heart racing, his breath shallow, the present moment dissolving into the warehouse floor. He had come to believe that proximity to others was proximity to potential abandonment or harm, that people were fundamentally selfish and would save themselves at any cost. The shame came when he allowed himself to remember fully. He had not helped the two who died. He had saved himself. Was he different from Derek, or simply luckier in where he had been standing? This question lived in his chest, and when it surfaced, the shame was so intense that he had learned to suppress it through sheer force of will-pushing the memories down, refusing to think about the event, telling himself it hadn't been that bad. But suppression required energy he didn't have.

When he returned to the retail position he had taken after leaving Brennan-a more modest role, but one that kept him away from warehouse work-he found himself hyperaware of his coworkers' small transgressions. A colleague who cut in front of him at the time clock, a manager who didn't acknowledge his greeting, a customer who was rude to another employee-each of these felt like evidence of moral collapse, proof that the world was full of people like Derek. His vigilance became exhausting. Colleagues began to notice that Luca seemed distant, occasionally hostile to minor infractions that would normally go unremarked. At work, he had also begun to avoid situations where he felt trapped: he would not take the elevator at the mall, he parked his car near exits, and he found himself scanning every room he entered for secondary exits-the stockroom, the break room, even the bathroom-a habit so ingrained now that he barely noticed doing it anymore. His manager had mentioned, gently, that Luca seemed "on edge" and had suggested he take some time off, but Luca knew that time away would only give the memories more space to grow. His daughter had stopped asking him to play the games they used to play together; she seemed to sense his distance, his mind always elsewhere, always calculating angles and exits. When the intrusive images came-Derek's face, the blackness, the feeling of being trapped-Luca discovered that physical pain could interrupt them. He would press his thumbnail hard into his palm, and the sharp sting would snap him out of the memory, replacing the thought of the fire with the immediate sensation of hurt. He held ice against his skin until his fingers burned, anything to force his mind away from what he had witnessed and what he had failed to do. The pain was a switch he could control, unlike the memories themselves. Over weeks, this became his method: whenever the images started, whenever the shame began to surface and the thoughts about the fire threatened to overwhelm him, he would hurt himself deliberately, knowing that the physical sensation would drive out the trauma-related thoughts, at least for a while.

Maria had noticed the marks on his hands. She had asked about his withdrawal, his silences at dinner. Three weeks ago, when she found him in the garage pressing a lighter to his forearm, she insisted he see someone. Luca came to his first appointment reluctant, convinced that talking would only make the memories more real, more present. But the vivid snapshots were already there, and they were not going away. What he feared most now was that the shame would consume him entirely, that he would become the person Derek had revealed himself to be. What he hoped for, though he barely dared admit it, was that someone could help him understand whether he deserved to have survived at all.

vignette_attempts.vignette:
Luca Rossi was twenty-eight when the warehouse fire trapped him on the second floor of Brennan Logistics on a Tuesday afternoon in March. He had worked there for eight years, moving steadily from dock associate to supervisor—reliable, punctual, the kind of man his wife Maria called steady. A faulty electrical panel ignited in the storage section where Luca was conducting inventory. The alarm system failed. What he remembers now, with a clarity that exhausts him at thirty-six, is not the full sequence of events but a series of vivid, isolated moments: the smell of accelerant and burning plastic suddenly overwhelming; the sight of a coworker, Derek, deliberately kicking over a stack of pallets to clear an escape route, leaving two junior employees scrambling behind him; the texture of the rough concrete wall he pressed his palms against, searching for a door in the black smoke, feeling that grit embed itself into his skin. Luca made it out through a side window. Derek did not wait for anyone. Two people died in the stairwell.

In the months that followed, Luca told himself the story differently. He had been lucky. The fire was not as bad as the news made it sound. Derek had panicked like anyone would. But these retellings never quite stuck. The moments remained—snapshots, each one sharper than any ordinary memory. When he tried to think of his daughter's sixth birthday party from before the fire, the details were soft, almost watercolor. But the texture of that concrete, Derek's face as he kicked the pallets aside, the sound of the alarm that didn't work—these arrived in his mind with the force of something still happening. The intrusions came without warning: a smell of burnt plastic at a restaurant, the sight of a coworker in a red shirt like Derek had worn, the sound of a fire truck passing on the street. Each time, Luca's body seized as if he were back in the smoke, his heart racing, his breath shallow, the present moment dissolving into the warehouse floor. He had come to believe that proximity to others was proximity to potential abandonment or harm, that people were fundamentally selfish and would save themselves at any cost. The shame came when he allowed himself to remember fully. He had not helped the two who died. He had saved himself. Was he different from Derek, or simply luckier in where he had been standing? This question lived in his chest, and when it surfaced, the shame was so intense that he had learned to suppress it through sheer force of will—pushing the memories down, refusing to think about the event, telling himself it hadn't been that bad. But suppression required energy he didn't have.

When he returned to the retail position he had taken after leaving Brennan—a more modest role, but one that kept him away from warehouse work—he found himself hyperaware of his coworkers' small transgressions. A colleague who cut in front of him at the time clock, a manager who didn't acknowledge his greeting, a customer who was rude to another employee—each of these felt like evidence of moral collapse, proof that the world was full of people like Derek. His vigilance became exhausting. Colleagues began to notice that Luca seemed distant, occasionally hostile to minor infractions that would normally go unremarked. At work, he had also begun to avoid situations where he felt trapped: he would not take the elevator at the mall, he parked his car near exits, and he found himself scanning every room he entered for secondary exits—the stockroom, the break room, even the bathroom—a habit so ingrained now that he barely noticed doing it anymore. His manager had mentioned, gently, that Luca seemed "on edge" and had suggested he take some time off, but Luca knew that time away would only give the memories more space to grow. His daughter had stopped asking him to play the games they used to play together; she seemed to sense his distance, his mind always elsewhere, always calculating angles and exits. When the intrusive images came—Derek's face, the blackness, the feeling of being trapped—Luca discovered that physical pain could interrupt them. He would press his thumbnail hard into his palm, and the sharp sting would snap him out of the memory, replacing the thought of the fire with the immediate sensation of hurt. He held ice against his skin until his fingers burned, anything to force his mind away from what he had witnessed and what he had failed to do. The pain was a switch he could control, unlike the memories themselves. Over weeks, this became his method: whenever the images started, whenever the shame began to surface and the thoughts about the fire threatened to overwhelm him, he would hurt himself deliberately, knowing that the physical sensation would drive out the trauma-related thoughts, at least for a while.

Maria had noticed the marks on his hands. She had asked about his withdrawal, his silences at dinner. Three weeks ago, when she found him in the garage pressing a lighter to his forearm, she insisted he see someone.
